model_output.verdict: A dispatcher’s progression is clear, but the daily work needs more detail to stand out.
write_up: You’ve moved from warehouse work to Dispatch Assistant and then Dispatcher at Crossroads Regional Freight. That’s a clear direction, but a recruiter will likely move on because the current role lists duties without showing how much dispatch work you handle or what you do when problems arise.

Your line about tracking loads and updating customers is the best model: it names both the work and who receives the updates. Your experience is easy to follow, and the progression at Crossroads is worth keeping visible.

This is a common pattern on dispatch resumes, but duties alone won’t stand out in a pile. Let’s start with the current Dispatcher role and add the number of drivers or loads you handle, then give a concrete example of the road issues you deal with.

cards.line: Crossroads Regional Freight has no fleet size listed.
cards.cannot_tell: A recruiter can see that you work in regional trucking, but not how large the operation is. One brief company detail could give the dispatch work useful context.
cards.question: If you know it, how many trucks are in the Crossroads fleet?

cards.line: - Responsible for dispatching drivers
cards.cannot_tell: Dispatching drivers is the core of your job, but a recruiter can’t tell how many drivers you handle or how often you assign loads.
cards.question: How many drivers do you dispatch, and how often do you assign loads?

cards.line: - Track loads and update customers on delivery status
cards.cannot_tell: This names the work and the customers you update. The missing piece is how many loads you track and how often customers hear from you.
cards.example: Track [number] loads [frequency] and update customers on delivery status [frequency]
cards.question: How many loads do you track, and how often do you update customers?

cards.line: - Handle driver issues on the road
cards.cannot_tell: A recruiter can’t tell what kind of issues come up or what you do to handle them. One real example would show how you support drivers.
cards.example: Handle driver issues on the road, including [issue], by [action]
cards.question: What’s one issue you handled for a driver, and what did you do?

cards.line: - Use TMS software daily
cards.cannot_tell: Your skills section names McLeod TMS, but this line doesn’t say what you use it to do. Connect the software to your dispatch work.
cards.example: Use McLeod TMS daily to [dispatch task]
cards.question: Which dispatch tasks do you use McLeod TMS for?

cards.line: - Work with the safety team on driver hours
cards.cannot_tell: Working with the safety team could mean several things. A recruiter can’t tell what you do with driver hours or what you share with the team.
cards.example: Work with the safety team on driver hours by [action]
cards.question: What do you do with driver hours when you work with the safety team?

cards.line: - Helped dispatchers with paperwork
cards.cannot_tell: Helped leaves your part open. Naming the paperwork and what you did with it would show how you supported the dispatchers.
cards.question: What paperwork did you help with, and what did you do with it?

fit.note: Your experience points toward dispatch roles in regional trucking, with a progression from Dispatch Assistant to Dispatcher. Adding the number of drivers or loads you handle and examples of road issues would make that experience easier to assess.
